docs.text: Exceptions in a large C++ project ¶ The problem ¶ In C++ an exception is a type. What it means is decided by its place in a class hierarchy: std::runtime_error is a runtime error, io_error is an input-output error, and so on. This answers the question "what kind of error is it?". In a large program there is a second question that matters just as much: " where does it come from? " Which library, which part of it. A hierarchy handles that badly: To tell libraries apart you need a tree of classes per library. An exception class is fixed. The text and the fields that it can carry are decided once, for everyone. Boost.LEAF ¶ Boost.LEAF is a library from the Boost collection that approaches this differently: an exception does not have to be a tree of classes. It can carry any set of types , and every type is just a piece of information. The rest of this documentation uses LEAF the same way. Boost.LEAF in three ideas ¶ 1. A throw puts a set of types into the exception. leaf::throw_exception(library_A{}, part_1{}, e_what_info{ "library_A, part_1" }); library_A{} , part_1{} and e_what_info{...} are independent types. The exception now holds all three. 2. A handler asks for the types it needs. leaf::try_catch( []{ /* code that may throw */ }, [](const library_A&, const part_1&) { // runs only if the exception has both types } ); A handler matches when every type it asks for is in the exception. The other types do not get in its way. If no handler matches, the exception goes on. 3. Types can be added on the way up. auto load = leaf::on_error(library_B{}, part_2{}); While load is alive, every exception that passes through the scope gets two more types. Keep the object in a variable. If you drop it, the types are added and removed at once. That is enough to continue. The next page takes an ordinary project and uses these three ideas on it: A typical project .

docs.text:
Catching any set of types ¶ What we want ¶ The handlers so far listed the types that they wanted. A handler for library_A and part_1 is written by someone who already knows that such an exception may come. We would like one more kind of handler: one that catches any set of types, whatever is in the exception. It is for tasks like these: Check the agreement. Every exception must have a domain and a subdomain. If one of them is not there, say so. This is the problem of case 2. Report everything in one format. Print or log all the marks that arrived, whichever they are. Do something specific. For example, count errors per library, or map the marks to an exit code. A handler that takes types by reference cannot do this. It matches only when all its types are there, and it cannot ask which types are missing. Catch by pointers ¶ LEAF has a way: a handler may take its parameters by pointer . leaf::try_catch( []{ function_lib_B_part_1_miss_domain(); }, []( const exception::domain::library_A* domain_a, const exception::domain::library_B* domain_b, const exception::domain::library_C* domain_c, const exception::subdomain::library_B::part_1* subdomain_b_1, const exception::e_what_info* info ) { if (!domain_a && !domain_b && !domain_c) { std::cout << "ERROR: no domain in exception!
"; } if (subdomain_b_1) { std::cout << "subdomain: library_B::part_1
"; } if (info) { std::cout << "what: " << info->what << '
'; } } ); ERROR: no domain in exception! subdomain: library_B::part_1 what: library_B, part_1 A pointer handler always matches . A type that is in the exception arrives as a valid pointer. A type that is not in the exception arrives as nullptr . So the handler can see what is there, and also what is missing. This is the case 2 of the previous page: the forgotten domain is now a message. What is still awkward ¶ The pointer handler solves the problem, but writing it everywhere is not comfortable: It matches everything, so it must come last , after the handlers of the types that you do know. The list of pointers is long, and every place that needs it has to repeat it. It is a handler like any other. Whether the exception then stays here or goes up is something that every place decides on its own. We would like the list to live in one place, to be checked by the compiler, and the decision "swallow or pass up" to be explicit. That is what the next page is about: leaf_spy .

Getting started ¶ Requirements ¶ C++20 (concepts and fold expressions) Boost.LEAF. If the target Boost::leaf does not exist when the library is configured, the library fetches boostorg/leaf itself. The library is header-only. The only target is the INTERFACE library leaf_spy::leaf_spy . CMake ¶ The library lives at github.com/goloveshin/leaf_spy . Fetch it with FetchContent : include(FetchContent) FetchContent_Declare( leaf_spy GIT_REPOSITORY https://github.com/goloveshin/leaf_spy.git GIT_TAG main ) FetchContent_MakeAvailable(leaf_spy) target_link_libraries(my_app PRIVATE leaf_spy::leaf_spy) Replace main with a release tag to pin a version. To use a local copy instead, replace GIT_REPOSITORY and GIT_TAG with SOURCE_DIR <path> . The library has an option LEAF_SPY_BUILD_TESTS . It builds the unit tests and the example of the library. It is ON only when leaf_spy is the top-level project, so a project that uses the library does not build them. You can set it yourself before FetchContent_MakeAvailable : set(LEAF_SPY_BUILD_TESTS OFF) The first program ¶ #include <leaf_spy.hpp> #include <boost/leaf/exception.hpp> #include <iostream> #include <string> namespace leaf = boost::leaf; struct library_A{}; struct part_1{}; struct e_what_info { std::string what; }; struct spy_t { // the slot types the context keeps void operator()(const library_A*, const part_1*, const e_what_info*) const { } // reads the slots of the exception template <typename Context> void visit(Context& ctx, const leaf::error_id id, std::exception*) const { if (ctx.template get<library_A>(id)) { std::cout << "domain: library_A
"; } if (ctx.template get<part_1>(id)) { std::cout << "subdomain: part_1
"; } if (const auto* info = ctx.template get<e_what_info>(id)) { std::cout << "what: " << info->what << '
'; } } }; int main() { leaf_spy::try_catch( { .job_that_may_throw = [] { leaf::throw_exception(library_A{}, part_1{}, e_what_info{ "disk is full" }); }, .notify_that_job_executed_with_throw = []{}, .notify_that_job_executed_without_throw = []{}, .is_throw_out = false }, spy_t{} ); } Output: domain: library_A subdomain: part_1 what: disk is full Three parts, in the order they appear: Marks. library_A , part_1 , e_what_info are plain structs, as in A typical project . Spy. spy_t has an operator() that lists the marks to keep, and a visit that reads them. See The spy handler . try_catch . It runs the job. Nothing handled the exception, so the spy runs. is_throw_out = false keeps the exception inside.

docs.text: Direct handlers ¶ Besides the spy, try_catch accepts any number of direct handlers. They are the handlers of leaf::try_catch , with the same rules as in A typical project . try_catch( args, spy, [](const exception::domain::library_C&, const exception::subdomain::library_C::part_2&) { std::cout << "handled in library_C, part_2\n"; } ); A handler matches when the exception has all the types the handler asks for. What happens to the exception ¶ situation spy what leaves try_catch no handler matches runs the original exception a handler matches and returns does not run nothing a handler matches and does throw; does not run the original exception, with all its marks a handler matches and throws a new exception does not run the new exception Two details matter. is_throw_out ¶ Everything in the last column leaves try_catch only when args.is_throw_out is true . With false the exception stays inside, even after throw; or a new throw. The spy still runs in the first row. Use true in the middle layers, where you want the next layer up to see the exception, and false at the top, where the exception ends. throw; against a new exception ¶ throw; is the normal way to say "I looked, but it is not for me". The original exception goes up, and the marks go with it. The next try_catch up sees the same marks. Throwing something else, for example std::runtime_error , replaces the exception. The marks of the original are not passed on. The two cases are told apart by the address of the exception object. If the handler rethrows the very object that was caught, it is the original. A handler that does not match ¶ A handler that asks for a mark the exception does not have is skipped. The common mistake is a wrong subdomain: // the exception has part_3, the handler asks for part_2 [](const exception::domain::library_C&, const exception::subdomain::library_C::part_2&) { } The exception goes to the spy and up. It is the same as case 5 of the typical project, with the spy added.

docs.text:
A typical project ¶ Libraries and their parts ¶ Imagine an ordinary C++ project. It is built from libraries. Every library has a few parts that matter: a module, a layer, a component. Here there are three libraries, library_A , library_B , library_C , with one to four parts each. Where does the exception come from? ¶ Code of one library calls code of another. When something fails deep inside, an exception travels up through all of them and arrives at the top. By then the type and the text rarely say where it started. We want to know: which library, which part . Domains, subdomains and marks ¶ The answer is to let every throw say where it is from. Two names help to talk about it: a domain is the library the code belongs to a subdomain is the part of that library and the information itself is a mark : an empty struct that you put into the exception. It carries no data. Its type is the information. Note Nothing is invented here. A mark is an ordinary Boost.LEAF type that is put into an exception, exactly as in the first of the three ideas . "Domain" and "subdomain" are only names for two groups of such types that turn out to be useful for a project made of libraries. Declare the marks in one header ¶ Keep every mark in one header, so that the throwing code and the catching code agree: namespace exception { namespace domain { struct library_A{}; struct library_B{}; struct library_C{}; }// namespace domain namespace subdomain { namespace library_A { struct part_1{}; } namespace library_B { struct part_1{}; struct part_2{}; } namespace library_C { struct part_1{}; struct part_2{}; struct part_3{}; struct part_4{}; } }// namespace subdomain namespace details { struct special_data_t{}; }// namespace details struct e_what_info { std::string what; }; }// namespace exception group meaning domain the library subdomain a part of a library details clarifying details, anything you need e_* structs payloads with data, such as a text or a path The agreement ¶ We add one rule: An exception must contain a domain and a subdomain. It is only an agreement. Nothing in C++ or LEAF checks it. Keep it in mind, because the next cases show where it gets lost. Six situations ¶ All six use only Boost.LEAF. The functions are code of the three libraries. The top of the program calls them under leaf::try_catch . Case 1: a plain throw ¶ A function of library_A throws with its domain, its subdomain and a text: void function_lib_A_part_1() { leaf::throw_exception( exception::domain::library_A{}, exception::subdomain::library_A::part_1{}, exception::e_what_info{ "library_A, part_1" } ); } The caller handles it with a handler that asks for those types: leaf::try_catch( []{ function_lib_A_part_1(); }, []( const exception::domain::library_A&, const exception::subdomain::library_A::part_1&, const exception::e_what_info& info ) { std::cout << "caught in library_A, part_1: " << info.what << '
'; } ); caught in library_A, part_1: library_A, part_1 Case 2: a domain is forgotten ¶ A function of library_B forgets the domain: void function_lib_B_part_1_miss_domain() { leaf::throw_exception( exception::subdomain::library_B::part_1{}, exception::e_what_info{ "library_B, part_1" } ); } A handler that asks for the domain and the subdomain of library_B does not match: try { leaf::try_catch( []{ function_lib_B_part_1_miss_domain(); }, [](const exception::domain::library_B&, const exception::subdomain::library_B::part_1&) { std::cout << "caught in library_B, part_1
"; } ); } catch (const std::exception&) { std::cout << "nobody handled it, and nobody said why
"; } nobody handled it, and nobody said why The agreement is broken, and no one noticed. The exception just flew past every handler. This is the first thing that we will want to fix. Case 3: an exception gets the marks of a second domain ¶ A function of library_B calls a callback that comes from library_C . It adds its own marks with leaf::on_error : void function_lib_B_part_2_execute_callback(std::function<void()> callback) { // attach the domain and subdomain of the place that called the callback auto load = leaf::on_error( exception::domain::library_B{}, exception::subdomain::library_B::part_2{} ); callback(); } The callback comes from library_C and throws with its own marks: std::function<void()> function_lib_C_part_1_get_callback() { return [] { leaf::throw_exception( exception::domain::library_C{}, exception::subdomain::library_C::part_1{}, exception::e_what_info{ "callback from library_C, part_1" } ); }; } The exception passes through two places, and carries the marks of both: leaf::try_catch( [] { function_lib_B_part_2_execute_callback(function_lib_C_part_1_get_callback()); }, []( const exception::domain::library_B&, const exception::subdomain::library_B::part_2&, const exception::domain::library_C&, const exception::subdomain::library_C::part_1& ) { std::cout << "caught: library_C, part_1 called from library_B, part_2
"; } ); caught: library_C, part_1 called from library_B, part_2 So the exception tells not only where it started, but also who called. Case 4: a library handles its own exception ¶ A function of library_C catches its own exception inside: void function_lib_C_part_2() { leaf::try_catch( [] { leaf::throw_exception( exception::domain::library_C{}, exception::subdomain::library_C::part_2{}, exception::e_what_info{ "library_C, part_2" } ); }, [](const exception::domain::library_C&, const exception::subdomain::library_C::part_2&) { std::cout << "handled inside library_C, part_2
"; } ); } handled inside library_C, part_2 The handler returned, and the exception is over. Nothing reaches the caller. Case 5: a handler does not match ¶ The same shape, but the handler asks for part_2 while the exception has part_3 : void function_lib_C_part_3() { leaf::try_catch( [] { leaf::throw_exception( exception::domain::library_C{}, exception::subdomain::library_C::part_3{}, exception::e_what_info{ "library_C, part_3" } ); }, // asks for part_2, but the exception has part_3 [](const exception::domain::library_C&, const exception::subdomain::library_C::part_2&) { std::cout << "handled inside library_C, part_3
"; } ); } The handler does not match, so the exception goes up with all its marks. The caller handles it: leaf::try_catch( []{ function_lib_C_part_3(); }, [](const exception::domain::library_C&, const exception::subdomain::library_C::part_3&) { std::cout << "main: caught library_C, part_3
"; } ); main: caught library_C, part_3 Case 6: a handler looks and passes it up ¶ A handler matches, does something, and rethrows with throw; : void function_lib_C_part_4() { leaf::try_catch( [] { leaf::throw_exception( exception::domain::library_C{}, exception::subdomain::library_C::part_4{}, exception::details::special_data_t{}, exception::e_what_info{ "library_C, part_4" } ); }, [](const exception::details::special_data_t&) { std::cout << "inner handler: special data, pass it up
"; throw; } ); } The caller still sees all the marks: leaf::try_catch( []{ function_lib_C_part_4(); }, [](const exception::domain::library_C&, const exception::subdomain::library_C::part_4&) { std::cout << "main: caught library_C, part_4
"; } ); inner handler: special data, pass it up main: caught library_C, part_4 What we have, and what is missing ¶ With Boost.LEAF alone we can mark the exceptions of a project, add marks on the way up, handle by marks, and pass an exception on. Case 2 showed what is missing: nobody noticed that a mark was not there. The next page is about that: Catching any set of types .

It adds its own marks with leaf::on_error : void function_lib_B_part_2_execute_callback(std::function<void()> callback) { // attach the domain and subdomain of the place that called the callback auto load = leaf::on_error( exception::domain::library_B{}, exception::subdomain::library_B::part_2{} ); callback(); } The callback comes from library_C and throws with its own marks: std::function<void()> function_lib_C_part_1_get_callback() { return [] { leaf::throw_exception( exception::domain::library_C{}, exception::subdomain::library_C::part_1{}, exception::e_what_info{ "callback from library_C, part_1" } ); }; } The exception passes through two places, and carries the marks of both: leaf::try_catch( [] { function_lib_B_part_2_execute_callback(function_lib_C_part_1_get_callback()); }, []( const exception::domain::library_B&, const exception::subdomain::library_B::part_2&, const exception::domain::library_C&, const exception::subdomain::library_C::part_1& ) { std::cout << "caught: library_C, part_1 called from library_B, part_2\n"; } ); caught: library_C, part_1 called from library_B, part_2 So the exception tells not only where it started, but also who called.
docs.title: Case 3: an exception gets the marks of a second domain

docs.text: A function of library_C catches its own exception inside: void function_lib_C_part_2() { leaf::try_catch( [] { leaf::throw_exception( exception::domain::library_C{}, exception::subdomain::library_C::part_2{}, exception::e_what_info{ "library_C, part_2" } ); }, [](const exception::domain::library_C&, const exception::subdomain::library_C::part_2&) { std::cout << "handled inside library_C, part_2\n"; } ); } handled inside library_C, part_2 The handler returned, and the exception is over. Nothing reaches the caller.
docs.title: Case 4: a library handles its own exception

docs.text: The same shape, but the handler asks for part_2 while the exception has part_3 : void function_lib_C_part_3() { leaf::try_catch( [] { leaf::throw_exception( exception::domain::library_C{}, exception::subdomain::library_C::part_3{}, exception::e_what_info{ "library_C, part_3" } ); }, // asks for part_2, but the exception has part_3 [](const exception::domain::library_C&, const exception::subdomain::library_C::part_2&) { std::cout << "handled inside library_C, part_3\n"; } ); } The handler does not match, so the exception goes up with all its marks. The caller handles it: leaf::try_catch( []{ function_lib_C_part_3(); }, [](const exception::domain::library_C&, const exception::subdomain::library_C::part_3&) { std::cout << "main: caught library_C, part_3\n"; } ); main: caught library_C, part_3
docs.title: Case 5: a handler does not match

docs.text: A handler matches, does something, and rethrows with throw; : void function_lib_C_part_4() { leaf::try_catch( [] { leaf::throw_exception( exception::domain::library_C{}, exception::subdomain::library_C::part_4{}, exception::details::special_data_t{}, exception::e_what_info{ "library_C, part_4" } ); }, [](const exception::details::special_data_t&) { std::cout << "inner handler: special data, pass it up\n"; throw; } ); } The caller still sees all the marks: leaf::try_catch( []{ function_lib_C_part_4(); }, [](const exception::domain::library_C&, const exception::subdomain::library_C::part_4&) { std::cout << "main: caught library_C, part_4\n"; } ); inner handler: special data, pass it up main: caught library_C, part_4
docs.title: Case 6: a handler looks and passes it up

docs.text: With Boost.LEAF alone we can mark the exceptions of a project, add marks on the way up, handle by marks, and pass an exception on. Case 2 showed what is missing: nobody noticed that a mark was not there. The next page is about that: Catching any set of types .

docs.text: leaf_spy ¶ leaf_spy is the solution to what the previous pages wanted. It is a small header-only wrapper around Boost.LEAF. It gives you one function, try_catch . try_catch is leaf::try_catch plus one more handler, the Spy : First your handlers try, by reference, exactly as in leaf::try_catch . If none of them matched, the Spy gets the exception. The Spy is the catch-all handler by pointers from the previous page, moved into one reusable object. It sees any set of types. A flag, is_throw_out , says whether the exception stays inside try_catch or goes up. What you get ¶ The list of marks lives in one place. The Spy is a small struct. Its operator() lists the marks, and the compiler checks that every one is a pointer. A catch-all that is always last. You do not have to order handlers by hand. The Spy runs only when no other handler matched. A clear decision what leaves. A handler can swallow the exception, pass the original up with throw; , or throw a new one. is_throw_out turns all of these on or off at once. Threads. captured_leaf_exception carries the marks from a worker thread to the thread that catches. Where to read next ¶ If you want to... Read build it and run the first program Getting started print or log the marks of any exception The spy handler catch some exceptions yourself Direct handlers use it with threads Threads use it in unit tests Testing look up an exact signature Reference

docs.text: The spy handler ¶ The spy is the object that reads the marks of an exception that nobody handled. It is the second argument of try_catch . A spy has two members. operator() : which marks to keep ¶ void operator()( const exception::domain::library_A*, const exception::domain::library_B*, const exception::subdomain::library_A::part_1*, const exception::e_what_info* ) const { } The body is empty. Only the parameter list matters: Boost.LEAF looks at it and reserves a slot for every type in it. A mark that is not listed here is not kept, and visit will not find it. Every parameter must be a pointer. try_catch checks this at compile time with SpyHandlerConcept . visit : read them ¶ template <typename Context> void visit( Context& ctx, const leaf::error_id id, std::exception* exception ) const ctx.template get<T>(id) returns a pointer to the mark of type T , or nullptr if the exception does not have it. const auto* domain_a = ctx.template get<exception::domain::library_A>(id); if (domain_a) { ss << "domain: library_A\n"; } exception is the caught std::exception . It is nullptr if the thrown object was not derived from std::exception . What a spy usually does ¶ A spy for a project built with domains and subdomains (see A typical project ) usually does four things: prints the std::exception text prints every domain and subdomain it finds, and an error line if there is none of one kind prints the payloads, such as the e_what_info text prints Boost.LEAF's own diagnostic info The check of the agreement "an exception must contain a domain and a subdomain" lives here. It is the pointer handler from Catching any set of types , written once: const auto* domain_a = ctx.template get<exception::domain::library_A>(id); const auto* domain_b = ctx.template get<exception::domain::library_B>(id); const auto* domain_c = ctx.template get<exception::domain::library_C>(id); if (!domain_a && !domain_b && !domain_c) { out << "ERROR: no domain in exception!\n"; } Output goes where you choose ¶ The spy writes where you want. It can hold a std::ostringstream by reference and let you print it later, write to std::cout , or send the text to a log. One spy per project ¶ All spies in a program usually share the same list of marks, so declare one and reuse it. The unit tests use a small one of their own, see Testing .

docs.text: Testing ¶ Two things are worth testing: that your code throws the right marks, and that handlers react as you expect. Both use try_catch with a small spy that records what it saw. The unit tests of the library use doctest , but nothing here depends on it. A recording spy ¶ struct mark_a { int value = 0; }; struct mark_b { int value = 0; }; // a type the exception never has: a handler for it never matches struct bottom_skip_t{}; struct seen_marks_t { bool saw_a = false; int a = 0; }; struct bind_t { seen_marks_t* marks = nullptr; void operator()(const mark_a*, const mark_b*) const { } template <typename Context> void visit(Context& ctx, const leaf::error_id id, std::exception*) const { if (const auto* a = ctx.template get<mark_a>(id)) { marks->saw_a = true; marks->a = a->value; } } }; A helper for the arguments ¶ leaf_spy_args_t make_args( const leaf_spy_args_t::job_that_may_throw_ft& job, const bool is_throw_out ) { return leaf_spy_args_t{ .job_that_may_throw = job, .notify_that_job_executed_with_throw = on_throw, .notify_that_job_executed_without_throw = on_ok, .is_throw_out = is_throw_out }; } on_throw and on_ok are const empty functions of the matching types. They must outlive the call, because the arguments hold references. A test ¶ TEST_CASE("is_throw_out false swallows when no direct handler matches") { seen_marks_t marks; const leaf_spy_args_t::job_that_may_throw_ft job = [] { leaf::throw_exception(std::runtime_error("job"), mark_a{ 11 }, mark_b{ 22 }); }; CHECK_NOTHROW((try_catch( make_args(job, false), bind_t{ &marks }, [](const bottom_skip_t&){} ))); CHECK(marks.saw_a); CHECK(marks.a == 11); } Wrap the call in an extra pair of parentheses inside CHECK_NOTHROW and CHECK_THROWS . The macro would otherwise split it at the commas. What the library tests cover ¶ The tests in tests/test_leaf_spy.cpp cover each row of the table in Direct handlers : no handler matches, with is_throw_out true and false a handler returns a handler does throw; a handler throws std::runtime_error , with is_throw_out true and false two levels of try_catch , where the upper one catches what the lower one rethrew

docs.text: Threads ¶ Boost.LEAF keeps the marks of an exception in the thread that threw it. When the exception is rethrown on another thread, only the exception object arrives. The marks stay behind. This matters when a job runs on a worker thread, for example in a task graph, and the result is rethrown on the thread that waits for it. If no leaf context is active on the worker, the marks are lost. On the worker thread ¶ Capture the marks, and throw captured_leaf_exception that holds the capture: [[noreturn]] void fail(std::string what) { auto captured = leaf::try_capture_all([&] { leaf::throw_exception( exception::domain::library_A{}, exception::subdomain::library_A::part_1{}, exception::e_what_info{ std::move(what) } ); }); throw ::leaf_spy::captured_leaf_exception{ std::move(captured) }; } try_capture_all runs the lambda, catches whatever it throws, and returns a leaf::result<void> with all the marks copied inside. On the catching thread ¶ Nothing to do. try_catch catches captured_leaf_exception , calls result->value() and the marks are loaded into its context. Direct handlers and the spy then see them as if the exception had been thrown here. Details ¶ captured_leaf_exception is std::exception -derived, so it travels through the usual machinery ( std::exception_ptr , futures). The result is held by a std::shared_ptr , so copying the exception is cheap. If the job itself runs on the catching thread, none of this is needed.
